title: Smile and House
premise: Cyrus Almeida hosts the graveyard shift at a failing AM station, taking calls from listeners she slowly realizes died days ago—voices that beg her to keep broadcasting because something in her inherited house feeds on silence. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside beneath her property, Cyrus learns her grandmother didn't die of natural causes; she made a bargain, and the debt has passed down. To survive until sunrise, Cyrus must finish what her grandmother started: lure the thing back behind the door using the one bait it cannot resist—the voices of its victims—and pay the price of becoming the next voice on the line.
about_author: Lior Winterbourne is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent years answering calls from strangers in the dark before turning to horror fiction. They live in a coastal town where the fog rolls in early and every old house has a room nobody talks about.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. During her 2 a.m. broadcast, a caller describes his own funeral from last Tuesday; Cyrus assumes a prank but keeps him on the line because ratings are ratings. The emotional beat is weary professional detachment masking loneliness—she'd rather talk to a ghost than no one at all.

chapters.title: The House That Counts
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. She returns to the house she inherited from her grandmother and performs her nightly ritual: counting doors (eleven), checking locks, leaving lights on. A twelfth door appears where there wasn't one. The beat is creeping domestic dread—the familiar turned hostile.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV, intercut with call transcripts. More dead listeners phone in, each asking her to 'keep talking' and warning her not to answer knocks. Her producer Marcus thinks she's cracking up. The beat is isolation deepening as the living stop believing her.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Dario, foreman of the crew digging foundations for the county's new storm drains on the Almeida lot. His backhoe strikes wood forty feet down—a door, iron-banded, sealed shut from the inside. The beat is blue-collar skepticism curdling into unease.

chapters.title: Sealed From Within
chapters.summary: Dario's POV. The door's hinges are on the inside; the bolts were thrown by someone who never meant to come out. Scratches line the inner face—not trying to get out, but to keep something in. The beat is the dawning horror that the seal was a kindness.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Searching the attic for answers, she finds her grandmother's ledger: decades of names, dates of death, and airtime logged like debts being serviced. The final entry is blank except for Cyrus's name. The beat is grief weaponized into betrayal.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. A caller—the first voice, the dead man from chapter one—explains: her grandmother invited the thing across generations ago to save a dying child, and the broadcasts are the lullaby that keeps it dormant. Silence wakes it. The beat is terrible understanding.

chapters.title: Static
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. He arrives at the station to find Cyrus gone and the transmitter running unattended, playing a recording of breathing. Every clock in the building reads 3:33. The beat is the skeptic's world tilting—he heard his dead father's voice on the tape.

chapters.title: The Crew Won't Leave
chapters.summary: Dario's POV. The excavation site floods with fog that doesn't move; two workers walk toward the open door frame and don't come back. Dario bolts the site gate and drives to the radio station, because the voices told them all the same word: Almeida. The beat is survival instinct overriding pride.

chapters.title: Eleven Doors, One Lie
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Home again, she counts twelve doors now, then thirteen. One of them breathes. She realizes the house is rearranging itself around the thing's approach, and the real door—the buried one—is underneath her floorboards. The beat is claustrophobic panic.

chapters.title: The Debt Collector
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. The thing speaks through her grandmother's voice, polite and patient, itemizing what the family owes: seventy years of borrowed time, compounded nightly. It offers a renewal—sign the ledger, keep broadcasting forever, alone. The beat is temptation dressed as mercy.

chapters.title: Marcus at the Door
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. He reaches the house through fog that erases the road behind him, pounding on a door that opens onto the excavation pit instead of the porch. Cyrus pulls him back from the threshold. The beat is fragile alliance—two people choosing to believe each other.

chapters.title: Voices as Bait
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV, planning with Marcus and Dario. The dead callers reveal the thing's hunger: it eats voices, hoards them behind the sealed door. If they can make it follow a voice inside, the door can be resealed—from within, which means someone must stay. The beat is grim resolve forming around an unspeakable cost.

chapters.title: Rehearsal for Sunrise
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. They rig the station's portable transmitter in the pit chamber and test the plan; the dead callers agree to sing, to scream, to be loud enough to draw it home. Marcus begs her to find another way. The beat is tenderness under pressure—love arguing with arithmetic.

chapters.title: It Learns Her Voice
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. The thing begins calling the house phone in her own voice, asking to be let in, telling Marcus things only Cyrus knows. Trust frays; Dario nearly opens a door. The beat is paranoia—the enemy is indistinguishable from the people you love.

chapters.title: The First Hour
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, timestamped. Midnight: the operation begins. Cyrus broadcasts live from the pit chamber, the dead voices rising around her like a congregation, and the temperature drops as something vast turns its attention homeward. The beat is terrified exhilaration—the trap is working.

chapters.title: Behind the Door
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Inside the chamber beyond the door she sees them: every voice the thing ever took, standing in rows, mouths moving in silence. Among them, her grandmother, who mouths three words: 'Not you yet.' The beat is heartbreak reframed as inheritance—sacrifice was always the family trade.

chapters.title: Bolt the Door
chapters.summary: Dario and Marcus's alternating POV. On the surface, the plan wobbles: the transmitter fails, the fog surges, and Dario holds the physical door against pressure like a tide while Marcus restores power with bare hands on live wires. The beat is ordinary people performing extraordinary endurance.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Trapped inside with the thing wearing her grandmother's face, Cyrus discovers the loophole in the ledger: the debt binds a voice, not a body. She begins broadcasting her confession—the whole truth of the family bargain—to every listener, living and dead. The beat is defiance: naming the crime out loud breaks its exclusivity.

chapters.title: Everyone Is Listening
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Across the county, thousands wake at dawn to hear a dead woman's broadcast describing exactly what was invited in and what it costs. The thing starves as attention disperses—it can only feed on secrets kept by one. The beat is collective witness as weapon; justice outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. The thing, diminished, retreats behind the door; Cyrus throws the bolt from within as the first light hits—but her voice stays behind when she walks out. She survives, alive and mute-adjacent, her words now arriving only as radio static that somehow everyone understands. The beat is bittersweet victory: paid in full, changed permanently.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV, epilogue. Months later, she hosts the show again, doors counted, lights on, the twelfth door bricked over. Callers still phone in—some living, some not—and she takes every call, because someone should answer. Final beat: quiet vigilance as a way of life; the last line is her sign-off, 'Keep talking. I'm listening.'
